ai-at-work.title: Opaque recurrence, and other AI terms that you should probably know
ai-at-work.excerpt: The rise of AI has brought an avalanche of new terms and slang. Here is a glossary with definitions of some of the most important words and phrases you might encounter.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: TechCrunch published a glossary to decode the growing mountain of AI terminology that's now flooding workplace conversations. This matters because your C-suite is throwing around "opaque recurrence" and "prompt injection" like they invented them, and someone needs to actually understand what gets implemented in your collaboration tools and knowledge management systems. Here's the real talk: if you can't explain the technology your organization is betting on, you're already behind the eight ball on governance, risk, and making sure AI actually solves problems instead of creating new ones.

ai-at-work.title: Authors push back as publishers and agents make claims on Anthropic settlement
ai-at-work.excerpt: Authors say publishers seem to be claiming more than their fair share of settlement payments.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Authors are fighting back against publishers and literary agents who appear to be pocketing a larger cut of the Anthropic settlement than the authors themselves deserve. This matters to digital workplace pros because it's a live case study in how AI training disputes will likely play out across industries, and your organization probably has similar questions about data ownership and fair compensation buried somewhere in your employment agreements right now. Honestly, this feels less like a tech problem and more like a good old fashioned "who gets paid" argument that's been happening since the printing press, just with better lawyers this time around.

ai-at-work.title: OpenAI chief scientist argues for AI research slowdown
ai-at-work.excerpt: OpenAI Group PBC Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki called for an artificial intelligence research slowdown in an essay published on Sunday, after other prominent industry figures have expressed similar v
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Jakub Pachocki from OpenAI is arguing that AI labs should voluntarily pump the brakes on model development instead of racing full throttle ahead. For digital workplace pros, this matters because generative AI tools are already embedded in your collaboration platforms and email, so the pace of capability changes directly affects what skills your workforce needs and how quickly you need to retrain people. Honestly, watching a tech exec call for slowdowns is like watching a race car driver suggest lower speed limits, but at least someone inside the tent is pointing out we might want to see where we're going before the next sharp turn.

ai-at-work.title: Hackers steal $320M in bitcoin from Liquid Network, return most of it after patch
ai-at-work.excerpt: Hackers stole about $320 million worth of bitcoin over the weekend from a blockchain platform called the Liquid Network. In a somewhat unusual development, the attackers returned most of the haul earl
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Hackers grabbed $320 million in bitcoin from Liquid Network but handed back most of it, keeping about $47 million as what you might call a "consulting fee." This matters because your workplace probably stores sensitive data on blockchain platforms or crypto exchanges, and this shows even specialized networks have holes that can be exploited at massive scale. The fact that thieves felt generous enough to return 85 percent of the loot is either a sign they're honorable by criminal standards or they realized someone was about to patch the vulnerability anyway.

tools-tech.title: Sam Altman calls GPT-6 Astra rollout ‘messy’ as enterprise users wait for access
tools-tech.excerpt: OpenAI’s rollout of its GPT-6 Astra model ran into early access issues after paying ChatGPT users were unable to use the system shortly after launch, prompting CEO Sam Altman to apologize and say the
tools-tech.dwp_take: OpenAI bungled the launch of GPT-6 Astra, leaving paid users locked out and forcing CEO Sam Altman to apologize for the "messy" rollout. This matters because enterprise teams are betting on these tools for productivity gains, and launch failures erode confidence in vendor reliability when your whole workflow depends on something actually working. After 30 years watching software launches, I can tell you that a CEO apologizing on X is corporate speak for "our infrastructure wasn't ready but we're shipping it anyway" — which is basically the tech industry's greatest hits album.

tools-tech.title: 16 Gmail power moves for more efficient inbox management
tools-tech.excerpt: You might not know it from looking, but Gmail is jam-packed with time-saving tricks. Some of ’em are right there in front of your face, if you know how to find ’em — while others require a teensy bit
tools-tech.dwp_take: Computerworld rounded up 16 Gmail features and settings that can help users manage email more efficiently, ranging from visible options to hidden settings that need activation. Digital workplace professionals need to know these tricks because email management directly impacts productivity, and most people are leaving performance on the table by using Gmail like it's still 2005. After three decades watching people drown in their inboxes, I can tell you that half these "power moves" are probably things everyone should have learned on day one, but hey, at least someone's finally documenting them.

digital-culture.title: I coach world No. 1 tennis player Aryna Sabalenka. Here’s what productivity culture gets completely wrong about pressure
digital-culture.excerpt: I learned to perform under pressure at thirteen, sleeping rough on the street, where reading a room wrong could cost you far more than a meal—sometimes it was the difference between making it through
digital-culture.dwp_take: Aryna Sabalenka's coach argues that mainstream productivity culture doesn't hold up when real pressure hits, drawing from his experience managing performance in high-stakes tennis and surviving street hardship. This matters because digital workplace folks love selling stress management frameworks and productivity systems that sound great in theory but crumble the moment a major client deadline or crisis actually lands. The hard truth he's pointing at is that most of our fancy workplace wellness initiatives are built for comfort, not for the actual chaos of real work, which should make every workplace leader uncomfortable in exactly the right way.

digital-culture.title: ‘Did you use AI?’ is the wrong question. Ask ‘What did you use AI for?’
digital-culture.excerpt: At the end of July, a debut crime novel became the most expensive casualty so far in the publishing industry’s war over AI. Fourteen publishing houses had bid for the manuscript, with the winning offe
digital-culture.dwp_take: The publishing industry torched a $2 million deal when an author admitted using AI to write parts of his debut crime novel, sparking the usual panic about AI contamination. Digital workplace leaders need to stop treating AI like a virus and start building actual policies around how it gets used, because blanket "no AI" rules just push the problem underground. Turns out people care less about the tool and more about whether you used it to actually think or just to avoid doing your job, which seems like a lesson worth learning before your entire organization implodes over a chatbot.

digital-culture.title: America’s disposable workforce is growing. It comes with hidden costs
digital-culture.excerpt: Below, Paul Osterman shares five key insights from his new book, Disposable Workers: The Transformation of Employment. Paul is a Professor Emeritus of Human Resources and Management at the MIT Sloan S
digital-culture.dwp_take: Companies are increasingly shifting to temporary, contract, and gig work to dodge benefits, training, and long-term commitment while pocketing short-term savings. Digital workplace pros need to care because managing a transient workforce tanks knowledge retention, collaboration, and institutional memory, which no amount of Slack channels can fix. The real kicker is that executives saving money on benefits today are quietly building tomorrow's productivity problem, and no amount of workplace technology will paper over workers who have zero incentive to stick around.

industry-news.title: Philippines’ BSP Proposes 12-Month Payment Operator Freeze as QR Rules Tighten
industry-news.excerpt: The BSP is proposing a 12-month pause on new payment system operators as it tightens QR merchant identification and transaction-tracing rules. The post Philippines’ BSP Proposes 12-Month Payment Opera
industry-news.dwp_take: The Philippines' central bank is hitting pause on new payment operators for a year while it strengthens rules around QR codes and transaction tracking. This matters because compliance complexity directly impacts how your organization handles digital payments, vendor integrations, and financial workflows in that market. Honestly, this is what happens when regulators play catch-up: they freeze everything while they figure out what they should have required from the start.

industry-news.title: Cancel Microsoft 365 and Get Microsoft Office for Life for $50
industry-news.excerpt: Microsoft 365 costs $99.99/year, but Microsoft Office Pro gives you the same apps for life for only $49.97. The post Cancel Microsoft 365 and Get Microsoft Office for Life for $50 appeared first on Te
industry-news.dwp_take: Someone's selling perpetual Microsoft Office licenses for fifty bucks, which is half of what Microsoft charges annually for 365. This matters because it highlights the tension between subscription models and one-time purchases, and whether your organization's licensing strategy actually makes sense anymore. Here's the thing though: that "office for life" comes with no cloud sync, no AI features, no updates, and zero support from Microsoft, so calling it the same app is marketing fiction dressed up as a deal.

industry-news.title: This No-Code App Builder is Only $100 for Life
industry-news.excerpt: Swiftspeed's AI app builder lets teams ship native Android and iOS apps with no coding and no developer hire. The post This No-Code App Builder is Only $100 for Life appeared first on TechRepublic.
industry-news.dwp_take: A company called Swiftspeed is selling lifetime access to their AI-powered no-code app builder for a one-time $100 payment, letting teams build native Android and iOS apps without hiring developers. This matters because it democratizes app development for workplace teams who've been priced out by traditional tools, potentially shifting how organizations think about internal app budgets. That said, I'd read the fine print carefully and test it thoroughly before betting your business on a hundred-dollar lifetime license, because these deals have a way of disappearing when the company realizes their math doesn't work.

industry-news.title: TIOBE Index for September 2026: Python Drops Below 18% as Julia Nears Top 20
industry-news.excerpt: September 2026 TIOBE Index keeps the top 10 unchanged, as Python falls below 18%, C++ widens its lead over Java, and Julia nears the top 20. The post TIOBE Index for September 2026: Python Drops Below
industry-news.dwp_take: Python's market share dropped below 18 percent in the latest TIOBE rankings while Julia climbed toward the top 20, though the top 10 languages remained stable overall. For digital workplace folks, this matters because it signals shifting developer preferences and skill demands that affect hiring, training programs, and internal tool development strategies. Honestly, Python losing ground after years of dominance is like watching your favorite coffee shop finally get some real competition, except the new place serves actual science instead of just hype.
